newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Few economic fears as HK heads for China handover.
newsitem.headline: Few economic fears as HK heads for China handover.

text.p: Whatever fears Hong Kong people harbour about the handover to China, now only 16 weeks away, economic ruin is not one of them.
Some fear the heavy hand of the ageing Beijing leadership will gradual crush their freedoms.
Others eagerly look forward to the end of more than 150 years of British rule at midnight on June 30. For them the handover represents the end of a humiliating chapter of foreign occupation of China.

Many however are simply keeping their fingers crossed that it will be business as usual, that China really means to live up to late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's pledge of "one country, two systems".

The six million people of Hong Kong were promised considerable autonomy in running their affairs. Communism would not be exported south to fetter the territory's freewheeling capitalist ways which have brought undreamed of prosperity to a community built by refugees from communism.

Hong Kong could only watch from the sidelines as the outgoing British and incoming Chinese administrations traded angry words over Beijing's plans to scrap or amend laws on civil liberties and disband Hong Kong's elected legislature.
But they retained control of an important cornerstone of their destiny -- the economy.
Hong Kong's hardworking populace has few worries on that score as the clock ticks away.
When Financial Secretary Donald Tsang stands up to give his 1997/98 budget speech on March 12, a budget which will straddle the transition, he will be able to paint a rosy picture.

Last week, Tsang disclosed that the economy was expected to grow a solid 5.5 percent this year against last year's 4.7 percent real growth in Gross Domestic Product and reported that trade -- Hong Kong's lifeblood -- was improving.

"Hong Kong will start life as a Special Administrative Region (of China) in sound economic shape, with every prospect that we will remain the most attractive business location in this region," he said on Thursday.

His confidence was borne out by a poll commissioned by local broadcaster Asia Television which found that 80 percent of 552 respondents voiced confidence the territory would remain prosperous under Chinese rule, 15 points up on a similar survey in January.

Tsang, along with colleagues in the very top tier of the civil service led by the popular and influential Anson Chan, deputy to British governor Chris Patten, will stay on and serve beyond the handover.
Opinion polls show a broad welcome for the decision by Hong Kong's future leader, shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, to opt for continuity and re-appoint the powerful civil service chiefs.
But Tung, chosen by a China-appointed caucus in December, is not finding everything is going his way.
His view that political freedoms take second place to bread-and-butter issues has worried Hong Kong's vocal pro-democracy lobby.
"We have a spiralling cost of housing... mismatch of skills, education... these are the real problems which people care about," Tung said in a CNN interview on Friday.

Tung has denounced Democratic Party leader Martin Lee for "badmouthing" Hong Kong overseas during a marathon tour of Europe in which Lee warned that China's proposal to scrap or amend several of the territory's laws would erode civil liberties and cause incalculable damage.
Tung now plans his own tour of the United States to put across his view that the changes planned are merely technical and do not threaten civil liberties.

Martin Lee's Democratic Party, which is to be excluded from the China-backed provisional legislature which replaces the existing Legislative Council (Legco) at the handover, meanwhile vowed to fight on.
Party leaders launched a two-month-long fundraising drive on Sunday to fill its coffers and be able to ride out what promises to be a year in the wilderness after Legco is disbanded.
China's planned dissolution of the legislature and its replacement with an interim body will, at a stroke, undo the democratic reforms instituted by Patten to Beijing's fury.
The Democrats, who fared the best in 1995 elections held under Patten's revised rules, are determined to make a comeback in polls expected next year.
"The funds we are hoping to raise will also be used to contest elections that are to be held in 1998," Democratic Party vice-chairman Yeung Sum said by telephone.
